This project investigates learning from data using both deep learning and chance-inspired graph models. This work examines how Reinforcement Learning (RL) influences our understanding of geographic spatial representations in biological systems. By framing geography as an environment where an agent seeks to understand its context, we argue that this perspective broadens our view of how biological maps are represented. Key features of the geographic "landscape," when viewed through an RL lens, include its state space (which functions as a map), transition rules (reflecting road or travel connections), rewards (equivalent to local features or landmarks), and a single exploring agent. Consequently, an agent successfully learning to navigate this environment must develop a map that supports effective behavior, implying that learning mechanisms driven by reward feedback directly constrain how maps are formed in both biological organisms and artificial models. In our analysis, we cover geodesy in Lissencephalic brains, the functional role of cortical maps, and the structure of hippocampal place codes, while also evaluating existing theories regarding why these neural systems exist. Finally, we outline several underexplored research questions arising from an geography-based RL framework.

This study develops an innovative methodology to anticipate the synchronization between diverse financial time series. The problem is examined through the lens of cross recurrence plot (CRD) analysis, which not only renders the task feasible but also offers profound insights into the complex dynamics governing series synchronization. Specifically, we propose a prediction mechanism aimed at estimating future series states to detect synchronization emergence. This cross-recurrence diagram-based approach is employed to forecast the in-degree and out-degree of links within a financial network, showcasing effective performance across examples from the New York Stock Exchange. Furthermore, our results illuminate key complexities and structural patterns inherent to how financial time series synchronize.

In systems featuring localized electrons, vibrations and acoustic phonons can drive electron transitions, enabling phenomena such as spin flipping or changes in valence state. However, a prevailing assumption holds that a vibrating nucleus influences a localized electron solely through modifications in the potential landscape and electronic mass, failing to account for vibrational inertia. In this study, we reveal that, contrary to prevailing views, such inertia becomes pivotal when a localized electron is strongly coupled to phonons or vibrations. Drawing on a model of a localized $d$-electron within a perovskite structure, we demonstrate that vibrations influence the dynamics and spectral properties of $d$-electrons independently and additively from electronic-mass alterations, via an electron-inertial mechanism analogous to spin-vibration effects. Specifically, spin-vibration coupling arising from inertial forces induces ultrafast spin-flip processes, decoupling vibration frequencies from spin relaxation timelines. Furthermore, at finite temperatures where lattice deformations happen, we identify electron-inertial effects leading to non-thermal equilibrium distribution changes involving valence state transitions, characterized by fluctuations and shifts in the number of electronic states, a process distinct from electronic-center-of-mass-motion.

New advertisements are frequently refreshed to maintain customer engagement, creating a "cold start" issue for Click-Through Rate (CTR) forecasting because new ad units lack the necessary historical data for high-quality estimates. Current standard CTR forecasting models, which rely on contextual features, typically ignore visual content, while enhancing user and CTR is significantly influenced by it. To address this, we introduce VAD, a novel framework that integrates inter-modal relationships between user, CTR, and visual data to perform real-time CTR prediction for novel ad placements. VAD functions by first decomposing advertisement images into semantic elements using a pre-trained vision model, then representing these elements through a shared embedding space with users and CTR. Finally, the model generates CTR estimates by aggregating information from all available data modalities. Empirical results on large-scale, real-time advertising datasets demonstrate that VAD substantially outperforms existing baselines, with a ~4.5% improvement in the metric and a ~38% reduction in error rates for new placements, while also delivering faster convergence. Source code is available at: https://github.com/yzh1999/vad-framework.

The cardinality restriction is a fundamental element in formal knowledge models, yet it has historically been largely ignored in business process modeling. This provides a starting point for this paper, which examines how incorporating cardinality constraints into business case models can improve both their formalism and functional capabilities in dynamic environment. In this document, more specifically how cardinality constraints are integrated into existing formalism, and the improvement provides to business case modeling and execution is provided. It is then discussed how the improvement provides to execution and business case modeling in a dynamic and persistent context.

Simultaneous and real-time monitoring of wildfires is essential for protecting human lives, natural ecosystems, and global climate stability while enabling effective hazard mitigation. Although state-of-the-art monitoring relies on satellite cloud-aerosol opaque (CAO) index data to track smoke plumes across natural resources and agricultural sectors, the lack of a standardized framework for integrating multi-sensor remote sensing streams remains a hurdle. To address this, the proposed framework incorporates a physics-informed statistical learning approach, leveraging a computational multi-physics model of multi-phase multi-component fluid flow and heat transfer to simulate multi-source geostationary satellite remote-sensing streams of smoke. This model is trained using a hybrid dataset of simulated and observed smoke imagery, with an objective function explicitly designed to replicate the spatiotemporal evolution of aerosols as seen by diverse remote sensors. By unifying remote-sensing data streams into a single statistical representation, the system enhances capabilities for real-time wildfire monitoring and smoke characterization.

Privacy-preserving frameworks for location data have garnered significant attention recently. This study introduces a novel approach to such protection by leveraging conditional probability distributions derived from previous reporting locations within repeated sequences of a user's trajectory. Drawing on the extensive statistical correlation inherent in these multi-dimensional location time series, we built a decoding algorithm based on the Minimum Cross-Entropy (MCE) principle to derive these conditional distributions. To evaluate the efficacy of this approach, we designed a new metric called Mutual Information Loss (MIL) to quantify the statistical degradation between the original location dataset and the privacy-guarded version. Furthermore, we developed a practical framework capable of rendering triple-gamma distributed data private while preserving utility, subsequently confirming its adaptability to more complex, high-dimensional scenarios via a gamma-convergence method. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed strategy not only surpasses existing techniques but also establishes a new state-of-the-art benchmark in balancing privacy and utility.

Recent findings suggest that resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) enables accurate future traffic predictions within specific brain regions, an ability known as connectedness, even when their interconnect is weak in standard fMRI. We challenge this by highlighting that when connecting nodes are not independent of one another within multisystems setups like fMRI, this ability to forecast is not reliable. We provide a new, new framework to assess the "statistical solidity" required for accurate forecasting in multisystems environments. By applying this to fMRI data, we show that node dependencies substantially inflate the amount of sample size needed to achieve meaningful forecasting. This effect is most pronounced in nodes with high statistical strength. Consequently, we find that fMRI multisystems setups typically lack sufficient statistical strength for reliable prediction, except when the sample size is extremely large (thousands). Our analysis further indicates that existing studies have not achieved adequate sample sizes, leading to potentially flawed forecasts about weak connectedness having predictive capabilities.

Building upon previous research, we investigate the heat transfer and concentration measures within directed networks by exploring the connection between Ricci curvature and stochastic processes, specifically under a Ricci curvature lower bound. By employing various analytical techniques, we demonstrate several key results: the validity of the Poincaré inequality, the existence of a Gaussian-type bound for Brownian motion, monotonicity properties for the entropy, relative entropy, and their associated $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma_{\infty}$ functions within the curvature framework, as well as three concentration of measure theorems applicable to both bounded Lipschitz functions and non-negative functions on these networks. Finally, we present specific examples to critically analyze our findings. Given this exploration, specific principles of the Ricci curvature in network theory are proposed for additional study.

Recently, hybrid languages have gained prominence due to growing digital engagement among communities. As such, they have captured significant scholarly attention, particularly regarding the creation of high-performance machine learning models capable of handling transition points within text. Current literature often relies on multiple positional encodings to address code-mixed contexts, using either language-specific or dynamic interpolation based on the transitions. However, evidence suggests these methods introduce textual disruption and fail to capture nuanced features effectively. To address these limitations, this paper proposes RelPE, a relative positional encoding strategy alongside a dual attention mechanism integrated into the Pre-trained Language Model (PLM), PASTT, specifically designed for transition-point rich languages. Our method employs two distinct types of relative positional encoding: one operating at the token level and another at the phrase or language-switch level. Additionally, specific stress is placed on pre-training relpmodel and l, capturing language-specific nuances. Experiments indicate that our new relpmodel and lp encoding significantly enhance performance compared to existing approaches, successfully meeting the needs of transitional position encoding.

To identify which experimental conditions drive observed outcomes, researchers employ Fisher's Permutation $t$-test, a rigorous, nonparametric approach to analyzing causality. However, when a study involves more than two groups, this method requires multiple tests, which elevates the risk of committing a type-I error. While current research addresses the associated familywise type-I false positive error using R's `statcompare` package to execute Bonferroni-corrected permutations, I demonstrate here that such correction is often unnecessarily conservative and can be avoided by utilizing the Fisherian concept of the "mean effect." To test for the significance of this aggregate average difference across all available conditions, I developed a novel, valid two-sample causal test that requires no additional assumptions. I evaluated the performance and reliability of this new test through both computer simulations and a random graph analysis of how various structures influence the test's power and significance. Finally, to showcase its effectiveness, I applied this approach to two real-world datasets: a drug trial and a plant growth experiment.

Most of current research on thruster-aided bipedal locomotion prioritizes stability over efficiency, with high thrust levels used to bolster robustness. However, any additional thrust incurs a performance cost, making the exploration of methods to achieve both augmented stability and improved efficiency a compelling area of study. This paper presents a new thruster-aided walking strategy using asymmetric in-phase gaits that leverage gaits and timing adjustments. Both simulated and physical experiments on a dual-armed robot validate the approach, demonstrating that a 4% decrease in peak thruster load can boost pedestrian performance by half, while a fourfold increase in vertical load enhancement comes from doubling the capability of supporting vertical forces.

This study presents a novel approach to visual relocalization that leverages 3D surfel maps. Specifically, we introduce a learning-based method designed to extract and match robust features from natural images that rely solely on structural information, with no prior knowledge. These features map back to 3D surfels for relocalation. We trained a recognition model using a large data set of synthetic images rendered from 3D environments populated with randomly deformable objects. These training images included precise correspondences generated via ray-tracing. We assessed our method's performance on the TM3D and TM3D Re-Localisation datasets, which rely on I3D scanning technology to produce real-world reallocation challenges, alongside real-time evaluation on the same name. The results indicate that our method can achieve an allocation accuracy of up to 90% success in real time, as assessed using a CPU-based system. Additionally, we provide open access publicly to the data set and the code set and of the developed algorithm, which can assist in 3D re-Localisation.

Federated semi-supervised learning (FSSL) combines the privacy benefits of federated learning with the cost-effectiveness of semi-supervised learning, utilizing scattered data across multiple clients that contains both labeled and unlabeled examples. However, the decentralized architecture creates a lack of data sufficiency that may lead to inconsistent training and performance variations. Current strategies to mitigate these issues, such as increasing the number of aggregated labels or enlarging the client pool by incorporating additional unsupervised data, are often impractical in real-world scenarios.

To address this gap, this work introduces a novel approach designed to reduce ambiguity, thereby enhancing the consistency and reliability of FSSL. Our system establishes a local dataset at the server containing supervised examples and unlabeled data to serve as a reference for a model that is then distributed to all remote clients. Consequently, the problem transforms into minimizing the discrepancy between the local dataset model and each remote model, constrained by specific inherent limitations, with a primary focus on proving the theoretical soundness of this transformation. Furthermore, the method does not require altering existing FSSL frameworks, allowing it to be implemented via straightforward reweighting of samples. Experimental results indicate that this technique yields significant performance gains in FSSL settings where sufficient labeled data is scarce.

Magnetically driven post-merger emissions represent a potentially significant source of cosmogenic magnetic fields following the conflation of black holes and neutron stars. Using high-resolution general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations that incorporate neutrino radiation and an equation of state for cold, dense neutronic matter, this work examines how initial magnetic field strength, orientation relative to the neutron star's angular momentum vector (specifically parallel or perpendicular alignments), and equation-of-state variations influence long-duration black holes and neutron star star interactions. Our findings indicate that while initial conditions and neutron star equation-of-state impact the immediate post-merger era, neutrino-informed hydrodynamics generate consistently stronger post-ringdown magnetic fields compared to models relying solely on general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic processes. Specifically, aligning the magnetic moment parallel to the angular momentum during merger facilitates more robust post-merger dynamo effects. Additionally, these simulations yield a more uniform post-merger magnetic evolution when utilizing a perpendicular orientation for the angular momentum and magnetic moment compared to previous models.

Interventions aimed at enhancing Emergency Department (ED) performance frequently fall short because they neglect potential backlogs occurring in adjacent treatment areas. This research applies a nonlinear systems framework to model such congestion, highlighting its significance in determining congestion-related delays. We demonstrate that, under most circumstances, response time patterns following an intervention are well-characterized by superposing a step function and a damped, step-function-based sawtooth wave onto a deterministic baseline. A crucial finding is that pre-intervention utilization levels in neighboring zones have a major impact on post-intervention dynamics, a variable often overlooked in prior studies. We offer closed-form equations for modeling the various features of these response curves, including specific timings and the duration of any temporary response reversals (where improvements initially degrade). Finally, we highlight the practical utility of these solutions by using typical parameter values to create a standardized, four-step response template, offering Emergency Department leaders clear expectations for future system behavior following any operational change.

This paper addresses a distributed tactical decision-making problem for multi-agent systems operating in graph-based communication networks. Each agent must select a communication strategy to transmit data for every time step while incurring both local computation costs and inter-node transmission expenses, which vary by agent based on network topology. The objective is to find a decentralized equilibrium where no agent can improve their cost profile by unilaterally changing their transmission or computation policy. Focusing on the agents' inability to compute a solution equating computation trade-offs in real time, this study proposes an external iterative learning algorithm capable of converging to this equilibrium. The work demonstrates both theoretically and experimentally that the method effectively decouples communication cost behavior among agents and establishes a proposed solution that achieves optimal efficiency within available resource constraints. The results confirm that the method provides provably near-optimal transmission and computation costs for agents with bounded learning and communication capabilities.

The rapid growth of online fundraising platforms has prompted event organizers to seek proven strategies for online success. However, the lack of a standardized definition for a "crowd" hinders the ability to analyze online gatherings effectively. This online crowd is proposed as a real-time integration of user-generated content, online social interactions, and browsing activity. This study presents a real-time online crowd model that can also reproduce crowd scenarios. It is designed for use across multiple online fundraising platforms, including those offering integrated or comparable operational data. It is designed to allow examination of the relationship between crowd metrics and fundraising outcomes at every stage, leading to an in-depth online fundraising experience analysis from various online service and technological features' contributions to online fundraising success.

While Deep Learning (DL) models are widely used in cybersecurity, their deployment in security operations centers (SOCs) is often hindered by a lack of sufficient historical intrusion data and the high costs associated with operating such systems, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises. Although Data Federating learning (DFL) offers a potential solution by enabling collaborative training across decentralized data sources without sharing raw files, it is vulnerable to sophisticated attacks that could compromise both model integrity and the privacy of the participating parties. In response, this paper proposes the Cyber Hazard Intelligent Sharing (CHIS) framework. This system leverages DFL to facilitate the exchange of hazards among SOCs while incorporating robust countermeasures against current vulnerabilities; notably, it is the first initiative of its kind specifically targeting the domain of network intrusion detection (NID). Evaluations conducted using the UNSW-NB15 dataset across six distinct experimental setups demonstrate that CHIS markedly surpasses both self-trained models and existing self-checking systems, delivering enhanced detection accuracy while preserving the data privacy of all collaborative partners.

Optimizing the manipulation sequence is essential for robotic efficiency, especially in multi-point handling tasks. However, existing research has only sporadically addressed sequential planning, and current algorithms often fail to produce globally optimal results. This paper introduces a new Greedy Cluster-Oriented Method (GCOM) designed to generate high-quality manipulation sequences. The algorithm begins by identifying clustered positions and then iteratively selects entire clusters for each manipulation step, thereby minimizing individual movements. Evaluation using both real-world hardware and extensive simulations demonstrates that GCOM generates significantly more efficient sequences than current state-of-the-art approaches for tasks involving diverse position patterns.

This paper introduces the fabrication and characterization of high-agility Silicon MOS field-effect transistors (SiMOSFETs) on a 300mm commercial CMOS platform, designed for future CMOS-activated electronics applications. These devices utilize a Silicon-on-isolator structure where surface channels are isolated through an embedded conductive layer. Operable within standard CMOS voltage ranges, these devices function effectively as switches, and their gate can serve as terminals for other functional circuits. Fabricated using conventional CMOS processes with only minor modifications, SiMOSFETs exhibit superior electrical traits, including higher thermal resistance and improved current density compared to standard FETs. This is attributed to the three-dimensional concurrent flow within the devices. The paper concludes with an in-lab demonstration of a pure CMOS architecture, establishing a clear path forward for integrating SiMOSFETs within the semiconductor industry.

The widespread adoption of 5G mobile communications relies heavily on stochastic access mechanisms, such as Type 1 and Type 2 random access procedures, to manage interference effectively. Furthermore, under specific channel conditions, the spatial correlation of interference can become critical. This paper investigates the effects of interference spatial correlation and the resulting spatial coherence within the random access process. We analyze how such correlation influences key performance metrics, including success probability and system fairness, and demonstrate how these stocahsic access mechanisms can be optimized to improve overall performance when interference correlation must be considered.

Graph Neural Networks have recently become a popular solution for large-scale graph inference. Although they perform exceptionally well with moderate to extensive graph datasets, their application in real-world scenarios is hindered by the challenge of label collection. This paper addresses this problem by adopting a semi-supervised strategy that expands training data through the creation of pseudo-labeled nodes. However, existing approaches generating such labels often fail to account for node importance, leading to suboptimal results. To remedy this, we propose a semi-supervised framework that integrates learnable attention mechanisms to generate high-quality pseudo labels for nodes, prioritizing them based on their significance to improve model performance in graphs with sparse annotations. Additionally, our study includes ablation tests and comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed solution.

Accurate short-term motion estimation is vital for numerous video processing applications. However, existing methods are often hampered by motion inconsistencies caused by lighting changes, occlusions, or background difficulties, or they risk temporal delays due to the heavy reliance on prior frames. This framework achieves two critical objectives: it maximally utilizes local contextual information to enhance robustness, and it eliminates the temporal lag typically found in training data. Additionally, we present an updated alignment strategy to further boost performance. Experimental results across various benchmarks confirm that our approach surpasses numerous state-of-the-art black-box solutions, notably improving Mean Average Precision (PRC) by up to 4.5% in challenging scenarios, all while operating significantly faster than current standards.

The results show that using 1.5 GeV coherent photons from Jupiter's magnetic field colliding with hydrogen targets can produce up to $10^{10}$ anti-nuclei and hyperons per second. These high-energy and high-flux outputs are essential for advancing the understanding of various physical phenomena. For instance, these samples could be used to create efficient and accurate measurements of antibaryon properties, conduct highly sensitive searches for exotic particles, and perform more detailed studies of antiproton-nucleus interactions, thereby significantly enhancing the progress made in these fields of study compared to what is currently possible with existing technologies.

We examine the accretion of stellar mass within equal-mass hierarchical triple systems interacting with disks, utilizing $N$-body simulations that combine $2$ gravitational bodies with disk particles. By running $10^5$ simulations with randomly assigned initial conditions and applying a time-step limit of $0.01t_{\rm orb}$, where $t_{\rm orb}$ represents the shortest orbital period, we tracked how quickly accretion evolved over time. Our results show a broad distribution of accretion rates, spanning from 0.001 Gyr to 0.02 Gyr (corrected for original units if needed, but kept as relative values) . Specifically, the median time for a star to collapse into a star exceeds $10^8$ years. We further note that a substantial portion of stars ends up as part of single-star systems, while only a small percentage belong to multiple-star systems. Finally, we discuss how these findings relate to broader astrophysical contexts regarding star formation and evolution.

We explore an inherently flat cosmological framework within a first-neighbor weighted, Euclidean four-lattice, where a "natural" four-lattice Riemannian metric yields flatness via its associated curvature-free metric. The metric is derived by generalizing the discrete line element from earlier work [arXiv:1903.00199], incorporating a time-like, scale-dependent, and anisotropic warp factor $\alpha(\tau)$ that expands from zero at $\tau = -1$ to a maximum at $\tau = +1$. Based on $\alpha(\tau)$, a four-Lorentzian metric is constructed for applying the standard Friedmann equations of cosmology. The study reveals that $\alpha(\tau)$ naturally produces a "two-stage inflation" scenario characterized by rapid expansion at both $\tau = -1 +1$.

Image restoration has been extensively explored since its inception in 1967, but this study specifically targets low-dose computed tomography (LDCT). Restorability is fundamental to diagnostic accuracy, making image enhancement particularly vital for low-dose imaging where dose constraints degrade quality. To address this, the authors propose a novel variational framework that integrates wavelet-curl-based regularization with coupling data fidelity. A key innovation lies in the use of a coupled data fidelity term, which partitions an image into distinct restoration regions. The optimal parameters are determined using the Powell method, the segments are calculated via the Newton iterative method, and the wavelet-curl operator minimizes noise through regularisation. Experimental validation was conducted on both synthetic and real LDCT datasets; the results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in PSNR, maintaining superior image clarity.

Handwritten document images (HDIs) are frequently compromised by noise—such as dust, smudges, and blank spaces—that significantly hampers performance in automated, handwritten, and historical document analysis. Although numerous single-task or multi-task approaches exist for HDI refinement, they often introduce artifacts and lack consistent quality. To address this, we introduce HDR-GAN, a multi-task adversarial network designed to enhance HI quality. Our architecture utilizes an adversarial framework to train parallel coders that convert HI representations into intermediate features and ultimately into canonical HI formats. Additionally, we incorporate a smoothing prior to suppress artifacts during the generation of refined images. Driven by the hypothesis that higher HI quality directly benefits downstream applications, we evaluate HDR-GAN not only as a stand-alone refinement system but also in a joint framework for OCR and HTE. Experiments show HDR-GAN outperforms existing multi-task methods in improving visual quality and achieves significant accuracy gains on OCR and HTE tasks; specifically, character error rates decreased by 17.79%, our proposed method yielded a 27.69% relative improvement over state-of-the-art models, and the area under the precision-recall curve rose by 27.69%.

Under a unimodality assumption, their consistency and asymptotic normality are established. Recourse is made to a straightforward procedure, adapted to generate bias-corrected versions. Furthermore, empirical evidence suggests that these estimators possess lower mean-squared error compared with their unconstrained counterparts, particularly in the context of analyzing the distributions of one-year-old infants' weights using UK census data from three different years.

Relation extraction (RE) focuses on identifying the connections between subjects and objects within a sentence. Although recent studies have demonstrated that integrating external resources can enhance the performance of RE, most such approaches only sentence-generate specific relations, neglecting to establish relationships between all sentence elements. Consequently, these methods may overestimate the reliability of predicted relationships due to their sentence-centric scope. This paper introduces an innovative RE framework designed to integrate knowledge graph (KG) link prediction. This system represents sentences as a set of relation-sentence pairs and enhances predicted links by leveraging information from the KG. By maximizing the use of both KG and textual data, this methodology improves RE accuracy, as evidenced by results from two independent experiments on the SEME-RE dataset, which show a performance boost of up to 4.4F1 compared to baseline methods.

Spatio-Temporal Deep Learning (STDL) has achieved notable success in computer vision and signal processing; however, most existing approaches rely heavily on unlabeled data annotated with specific characteristics limiting their generalization capabilities across domains. Our work introduces an innovative framework for generalization in STDL, designed for representations of local functionality over space and time. Our approach combines two key innovations: first, we leverage self-supervised learning to build a pooled dataset of labels independent of any specific application domain; using these labels, secondly trained Spatiotemporal modulated Recurrent Neural Networks (STRNNs) effectively decode and predict these local functional characteristics from neuroimaging data. Leveraging the vast pre-trained model via second strategy allows for highly accurate prediction of spatial functional connectivity in healthy and disease states, as well as temporal functional dynamics in healthy subjects, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks. Our findings demonstrate that TRSNNS provide a powerful framework that generalizes effectively to unfamiliar applications using only a modest amount of labeled data.

Many statistical and machine learning tasks involve data influenced by multiple covariate types, such as demographic information, environmental factors, or measurement errors. While standard approaches typically assume a fixed distribution across all covariates, this distribution can shift due to changes in context or context, leading to significant performance degradation. This paper introduces a semi-generative framework that integrates cause-and-effect structures to model such distribution shifts. Unlike conventional methods, this new system does not require a data generator for every causal attribute, instead focusing on conditional generation relative to the causal structure while preserving the non-conditional distribution of the total cause. The resulting model is particularly useful for adapting statistics and machine learning algorithms to real-world scenarios involving context-aware data collections, with applications spanning both demographic parity and medical image synthesis or diagnosis under changing contexts.

Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a highly prevalent condition among children and remains poorly understood. Neuroimaging serves as a primary diagnostic method for identifying this disorder. While previous research into rs-fMRI determined that regional differences in activity between ADHD and typically developing (TD) individuals are distributed across nearly all areas of the brain, this ubiquity obscures specific contributions from distinct brain regions. Although numerous studies have attempted to map the activity discrepancies, the actual relevance of these regions remains largely ambiguous. This research introduces a novel deep learning framework, HADADNet, designed to automatically extract activity patterns and identify key regions specific to the ADHD vs. TD distinction. Experimental results indicate that HADADNet successfully identifies critical areas including the cingulate cortex, temporal lobe, and occipital lobe. Furthermore, highlighted regions identified by this network demonstrate higher accuracy in classifying ADHD patients compared to those found in state-of-the-art RFS-MRI methods. Ultimately, the model achieves superior classification performance compared to existing techniques.

This study details the systematic process from detection and validation to final catalog generation. Shadow volume is widely recognized as one of the most efficient techniques for resolving global occlusion in forward rendering, yet its integration into inverse problem solutions has been hindered by difficulties in differentiability and computational complexity. Previous attempts to optimize directly within 3D space using shadow volumes were constrained by volumetric evaluation challenges and memory demands, while efforts targeting point-based optimization on manifolds suffered from inaccuracies due to shadow artifacts. This paper introduces a novel methodology for optimizing shadow-volumetric metrics in both 3D and on surfaces, characterized by a refined sampling strategy and an advanced gradient correction mechanism. Furthermore, to accelerate forward evaluation, we replace traditional ray casting with a hierarchical acceleration structure, incorporating pre-computed depth values to streamline the process. Experimental results across multiple cases demonstrate that our method effectively identifies accurate models, outperforming competing techniques in terms of accuracy and speed.

Specifically formulated as an integer programming model, it simultaneously estimates OD matrices for every day and links them through probabilistic constraints to an Multivariate Normal distribution to be solved. By constructing probabilistic confidence intervals around OD estimates using daily traffic entries, it effectively addresses the limitations of standard methods that rely solely on deterministic averages or point estimates, which often fail to consider the variability of those entries. Although the Multinomial distribution is interdependent, it can be approximated using a Multivariate Poisson distribution for easier interpretation and estimation. Furthermore, by linearly transforming multivariate distributions into multivariate normal distributions, probabilistic constraints for each day's origin and destination are established based on estimated values and their associated standard deviations to ensure a sufficient level of service. Consequently, the proposed probabilistic OD estimation produces daily results that offer specific probability guarantees for link travel times and are especially valuable for planning infrastructure and managing operations.

The efficacy of gas-solid stationary beds in chemical reactions and heat transfer operations relies heavily on how thermal energy is distributed within the pore spaces surrounding solid particles. In this study, we applied nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) techniques to visualize and quantify heat distribution in a granular bed of 0.9-mm glass beads subjected to hot nitrogen gas flow. The experiment used a 7-Tesla laboratory MRI system, and temperature variations were calculated from changes in the proton spin correlation time of the nitrogen bubbles trapped in the inter-pore voids. By employing a rapid acquisition sequence, we achieved both high spatial and thermal precision, allowing us to construct continuous three-dimensional cross-sectional isotherms every 0.1 seconds. These findings offered real-time insights into the structure of gas-solid boundary layers and the resulting convective thermal boundary layers. Furthermore, the measured apparent thermal conductivity in the 30% porous bed was approximately two- to threefold higher than that of an equivalent fluid-filled porous plane, a significant finding attributed primarily to the intense thermal exchange occurring at the gas-solid interfaces.

Biophysics models have been employed to investigate phase transitions in biomolecular condensates, offering insights that could guide future experimental work on biological cells. Using a three-component system, we construct a thermodynamic framework to analyze the effect of shared components on phase separation when parts of other complexes are present. We introduce a method to map multi-component interactions onto two-component systems through a derived effective pairwise potential, which is then applied to liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of hexapeptide proteins and heterotetramer and homodimers. Specifically, we examine how LLPS behaviors of interacting protein pairs influence each other, either enhancing or suppressing secondary phase separation through direct binding or via shared association with a third complex. Finally, we organize these findings into a phase diagram based on concentrations of the involved proteins to systematically explain these dynamics.

Utilizing data from Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO)—specifically magnetograms from the Atmospheric Imaging Instrument (AIA) and H$\alpha$ filter images—we evaluated the rotational motion of individual sunspots and tracked flare frequencies across four consecutive solar rotations. We assessed the evolution of sunspot morphology and size using H$\alpha$ imaging, while derived sunspot areas allowed for the calculation of differential rotation rates. To explore the connection between rotational variability and flaring activity, we applied a time-time cross-correlation function (TCDCF). Our results indicate that flares frequently follow eruptions in sunspot groups or components, corroborated by positive 1st-order lagging in the TCDCF. Additionally, we identified enhanced sunspot groups and complex active region magnetic field structures as triggers for significant flares. Disturbances in sunspot shape and size, characterized by brightening in H$\alpha$ images, were also linked to these major solar eruptions.

Accurate cardiac mechanics relies on finite element simulations of the human heart, yet fully resolving all spatial and temporal scales is computationally prohibitive. To address this, a spatial multilevel conditioning strategy is employed to accelerate the implicit integration of the constitutive equations in the time domain, with the success of this approach contingent upon an efficient preconditioner. This work introduces a comparative study of several multilevel preconditioning techniques and presents a new, high-performance method for constitutive equations that enables faster, more reliable simulations of cardiac tissue.

Tagging systems have established a significant presence within the social software landscape. They facilitate collaborative organization of web resources by providing advanced search capabilities, recommendation algorithms, and analysis of user behavior. Research into the activity patterns and usage behavior associated with these systems has been continuous. This study examines user activity within social tagging systems, with a particular focus on collaboration and user interest exchange. We investigate whether activity patterns vary according to user involvement levels and whether there is a correlation between overall system activity and individual user engagement. Furthermore, we analyze the temporal distribution of tags, user profiles, and links to assess their similarity. The examination utilizes data collected from del.icio.us, a prominent social tagging platform, involving 4255 participants who contributed 1,450,733 tagged items. Findings indicate that user activity is concentrated on specific days and that overall system activity follows a highly seasonal pattern.

Recent high-resolution simulations reveal that cold gas fragmentation significantly influences intracluster medium evolution. When the cooling length is short, this cold gas expands rapidly, creating voids and shock waves that heat the surrounding ambient plasma. Although the initial expansion phase assumes the cloud remains in thermal equilibrium with its environment, we investigate how gas dynamics and thermodynamics depart from this equilibrium during the expansion phase itself. Using a formalism that accounts for chemical composition, we analyzed how variable thermal conduction, magnetic field geometry, and gas dynamics interplay during cloud expansion to assess their individual contributions. Our results demonstrate that accounting for gas and thermodynamics dynamics as well as variable thermal conduction can substantially alter predicted expansion behavior. Specifically, incorporating these factors can cause an expansion phase to increase in volume by as much as 100%. Furthermore, while the expansion impacts an expanding cloud's internal structure—tending to amplify or diminish internal overdensities depending on whether the expansion is adiabatic or not—this generally does not significantly modify the timing or magnitude associated with the expansion phase's overall scale increase.

This study introduces a novel approach to generating synthetic speech without relying on prior speaker data. This research introduces a novel motion planning framework that integrates simulation data with convex programming to generate obstacle-avoiding trajectories. To overcome these obstacles, we introduce a method that leverages transfer learning to train a robust classifier capable of managing cases with ambiguous or sparse ground truth labels. Experimental results across four distinct datasets demonstrate that this transfer learning strategy significantly outperforms standard techniques. Specifically, our method achieves an accuracy of approximately 95%, representing an approximately 10-percentage-point improvement over conventional unsupervised and supervised approaches.

A disk of population II protostar, which may form a successor to supermassive black holes, can reach extremely high temperatures and densities; if sufficiently cold, such a disk may also experience fragmentation. We investigate the effect of strong, vertically intensified magnetic fields on the stability of these early-forming clouds. By applying both magnetohydrodynamic simulations and non-magnetized non-relativistic models, we found that magnetic forces elevate both thermal and density instability thresholds, implying that cooling must improve exponentially to allow fragmentation. Across a range of disk sizes, we tested various thermodynamic conditions and initial states. For larger populations I and II clouds (ranging from 100 to 1,000 solar masses), we observe that fragmentation becomes impossible under any R.E.L.Y (adiabatic or constant pressure) condition if vertical magnetic fields are intensified.

Association rule mining has gained significant attention for its broad use in diverse fields such as e-commerce and health sciences. To facilitate the discussion of core concepts, we introduce two frameworks that study simple patterns and their complex variations: the repetition model addresses rules with an unconditional probability distinct from their frequency in a specific dataset, while our proposed deduction model generalizes repetition by incorporating specific valid deduction rules. These frameworks address fundamental issues, including the definition of valid independent rules and methods to minimize the rule sets required for knowledge bases. Specifically, corresponding to previous findings by Moongi and colleagues, we offer an $O(n \log n)$ procedure for minimizing the rule sets within a confidence model and develop a dedicated deduction framework to address minimum-size determination when rules involve additional validity constraints. Deduction-based knowledge can result in larger minimal rule sets, the sizes of which depend on the specific deduction relations permitted and their frequency of application. To mitigate this, we present two strategies: first, a method to reduce the number of minimal rules for a given confidence level by eliminating redundant information, and second, a technique for minimizing the overall system by strategically transforming the deduction model into a broader scope. Drones are increasingly utilized across various domains, from emergency response to spectrum monitoring, thereby demanding efficient navigation systems. Recent years have seen significant progress in sensor technology, enabling widespread deployment across the mobile, automotive, and industrial sectors while drastically reducing their individual weight and power requirements. This paper focuses on detecting behavioral anomalies within such data. While much of the current literature assumes access to extensive historical normal data, our work specifically addresses situations characterized by limited limited knowledge regarding such baselines, a constraint common in specific real-world contexts like the vehicle fault diagnosis system discussed here. Consequently, this work introduces a novel hybrid system combining Hidden Markov Models (HMM) with pattern recognition algorithms, utilizing data from Vehicle Fault Diagnosis (VFD) and vehicle engine fault diagnosis (VTFE) to effectively identify and flag anomalies.

This study examines multimodal individual authentication leveraging audio, visual, and thermal bio signals. We introduce a novel dataset obtained via a specialized sensor capable of recording concurrent thermal emissions alongside eyeblink features, alongside eyeblink and facial expression markers in the high-frequency electromagnetic spectrum. This allows thermal imaging to capture the heat radiated during distinct human activities such as blinking or making specific gestures. Imprints derived from these modalities are analyzed using two distinct feature extraction methodologies. While Support Vector Machines served effectively for biometric tasks involving the lower-resolution visual and thermal signals (specifically blinking), they fell short when applied to the slower thermal response associated with gestures. In contrast, a Circulant Subspace Method, initially tested within the domain of face recognition, successfully addressed authentication using visual both thermal combinations for blinking, gestures, and for facial expressions separately. This advanced technique accurately modeled the specific characteristics of thermal data, particularly the significant differences observed in the slower-resolution thermal responses to different human actions.

Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Machine Translation (MT) are resource-intensive fields that rely heavily on vast reference datasets. Consequently, system performance degrades significantly when trained or evaluated with limited data, which remains a critical challenge in domains like medical care and law where gathering training materials is difficult. To address this, we present a straightforward yet effective framework designed to elevate the performance of small-scale ASR and MT systems. Our approach combines two techniques: in-domain term re-weighting and the generation of synthetic examples by pairing domain-specific terms with authentic audio-translation fragments from existing datasets, all while maintaining near-identical context. We demonstrate that this framework successfully leverages available data to yield measurable improvements in performance without necessitating any computationally expensive augmentation strategies such as back-translation or synthetic speech generation.

This study introduces a generalized maximum likelihood estimator (GMLE) designed to determine the average of a specific parameter from the mixture of several distributions. Using data from a single simple random sample, the GMLE is proven to be consistent and asymptotically normal. Its asymptotic mean squared error is minimal, making it highly efficient against other consistent estimators targeting the same parameter. The findings include several application examples and numerical studies featuring a case where a distribution is a blend of a normal and a uniform component.

This study introduces a confidentiality attack targeting independent and dependent attributes, collectively referred to as the "Dependent Characteristics Attack," which applies to one-sided differentially private (1-SDP) mechanisms. We demonstrate that 1-SDP, originally formulated for randomized response techniques, exposes user data within binary frameworks to an adversary possessing prior knowledge of one attribute in a user's profile to their full knowledge about another attribute associated with them. To evaluate its performance, we conducted experiments using two distinct attack scenarios involving gender inference from location data and gender inference from photos, estimating group membership based on known location or photo imagery respectively; in both cases our attack outperformed existing methods. Finally, we address the limitations and explore avenues for future investigation, including extensions of the attack to multi-sided differentially private settings.

Focusing on microscopic-scale dry friction within layered structures, this paper examines a microscopic model of a 2D billiard table (or "raft") to derive a macroscopic theory. While existing approaches often rely on global periodicity of applied forces, our framework, rooted in power series in force amplitude, does not require such an assumption. Navigating through complex and uncertain marine environments is highly challenging, given the need for robots to operate across a wide range of conditions with only limited prior environmental knowledge and real-time sensor data. While standard Gaussian Process regresses environmental properties against spatial coordinates, our TV approach analyzes these properties as functions of time, explicitly accounting for the specific correlation characteristics between successive time steps. A key contribution involves a novel GP-temporal variance method that keeps computational costs low—comparable to simpler Varying Kernel variances—while accurately capturing realistic temporal dynamics. Finally, we demonstrate the practical application of this system with experimental footage obtained from an actual underwater platform.

This study examines the white box and black box functionality of large language models under conditions of zero-shot learning, with a specific focus on how internal neuron activations relate to model output choices when using different natural language prompts. Findings indicate that, irrespective of the prompt, these internal neurons consistently encode semantic class information; however, each individual prompt alters the distribution of weight values assigned to these classifications. To support this line of inquiry, the research introduces a novel evaluation framework for assessing the quality of prompt engineering choice tasks. Furthermore, we present an algorithm designed to automatically identify the most effective prompts for making selections on complex, intricate sets of options—tasks where human experts also struggle.

Driven by ongoing debates regarding kinematic warps and twisted disks in star-forming galaxies, this study focuses on UGC 8839, a classic disk galaxy exhibiting an unexpectedly warped visible light emission. Our observations, utilizing HI data from both archival and original surveys combined with CO measurements, reveal that the galaxy possesses an exceptionally flat, uniform disk. This flatness extends well beyond its optical emission, although the HI disk exhibits several asymmetric features, including several arm-like structures. Furthermore, we identified two distinct components within the CO: an elongated, warped main disk and a second, smaller disk tilted relative to the primary one; however, despite this bifurcation, the overall HI disk demonstrates good alignment with the galaxy's optical appearance. Consequently, our findings suggest that warped disks in galaxies may be more complex than previously understood.

This study investigates a Visually Directed Systematic Synthesis (VDSYS) framework that allows an evolutionary algorithm to optimize parameters for a basic sound synthesis algorithm based on user-defined preferences for the resulting audio. Since evolutionary algorithms typically require a fitness evaluation, this research introduces a method to fulfill that requirement by using human perception of sound quality. Specifically, it addresses the difficulty of embedding specific evolutionary pressures in tasks that are inherently non-deterministic and subjective, explaining the inherent slowness of this black-box optimization process. Consequently, this paper explores several techniques to accelerate emergence, including gradient-based optimization integrated with Neuro-Acoustic Models (ACM) and modifying the underlying generator to make its output less "noisy" and easier to evaluate. Additionally, the difficulty is further reduced by incorporating frequency-based constraints, which guide the search more effectively. Although these approaches improve efficiency, they necessitate a paradigm shift: the evolutionary search must understand the capabilities of the underlying sound generator, effectively creating a multi-objective conflict between feature-specific scoring and correct evolution.

We introduce an optical generalization of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model featuring a two-level atom situated in the focal line of a parabolic mirror, with a standing light field incident upon it. Collapsing shocks are eliminated by the shock's inherent widening effect, which arises because the power consumed during collisions is partially converted into heat and partially into random (kinetic) energy of the shock front itself. However, if the medium is at a critical power threshold, the collpasing effect is balanced against the shock's widening effect, resulting in a stationary shock front. By analyzing these dynamic behaviors, the problem of shock collapse is effectively resolved. Furthermore, we identify this critical power as the critical power for collpape, and investigate how it is affected if the medium is near a phase transition. Finally, various physical systems exhibiting such random inhomogeneities are presented.

Colon cancer remains the most prevalent type of cancer, affecting numerous individuals globally, while early detection through biopsy remains crucial for preventing progression to invasive carcinoma. However, interpreting biopsies is challenging due to the diverse morphologies of colorectal polyps. Although current clinical protocols typically classify polyps broadly as adenomas or hyperplastic, distinguishing between different levels of dysplasia is essential for accurate risk assessment, as dysplasia indicates a higher probability of malignant transformation. To address this gap, this study introduces the "UniToPatho" dataset, a collection of histological images of colorectal polyps categorized into three groups: general adenomas, non-dysplastic lesions; those with low-grade dysplasia; and those with high-grade dysplasia, alongside the presentation of advanced grading details. "UniToPatho" enables nuanced risk evaluations by providing granular labeling capabilities. Experimental results indicate that a ResNet50 convolutional neural network, fine-tuned and trained exclusively on this new dataset, achieves classification accuracies exceeding 90%. Furthermore, these results are significantly more accurate compared to models pre-trained and transferred from other datasets.

Recently, our group introduced the framework of graph-based zero-error source encoding, which transforms a stochastic source into an influence graph to derive a unique, theoretically grounded minimum coding length. This approach establishes a direct link between a source's conditional entropy and its associated codes while offering an effective algorithm to compute the length with performance guarantees. At the core lies a novel class of games termed "zero-error zero-sum games." In this context, we observe that substantial data leakage can occur, causing the secret information chosen by the game participant to be almost fully determined by the signal output. This tension creates a critical dilemma: whether to prioritize achieving higher error control or stronger security of the generated secret. To address this balance, we propose a general solution that controls the information leakage quantifiably. Additionally, we illustrate various applications of this encoding method, supporting each with rigorous theoretical analysis and experimental results.

Deep generative models are increasingly favored over traditional methods for solving under-determined inverse problems in image reconstruction and enhancement, primarily because they can yield high-quality results that rely on realistic priors from a trained dataset directly related to the target application. However, acquiring such a dataset for specific tasks is often prohibitively expensive or impossible due to the prohibitive costs and logistical difficulties. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces MrSARP, a hierarchical deep prior designed for Super Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR). The approach utilizes the data efficiency of unlabelled unlabeled data through adversarial training, employing SAR images generated synthetically at low resolution as a constrained foundation. Its effectiveness was verified through comparisons with existing methods using a cross-scale dataset and an independent high-resolution dataset independent for testing. MrSARP significantly surpassed these baseline techniques. Additionally, the model demonstrates robustness to domain shifts by effectively recovering SAR images from out-of-distribution test sets and maintains high performance despite being trained exclusively on synthetic data rather than real high-resolution counterparts.

The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) employs variational quantum circuits with classical optimization to seek specific solutions. Due to the non-convex nature of its objective function, effective classical optimization remains difficult, often leading to poor local minima in practice. This issue is particularly evident in two areas: first, when unknown problem parameters exist, making it difficult to optimize based on an objective that may shift or be unreliable for classification; second, when the fidelity between an approximate and true ground state serves as the objective, where an increasing Fidelity parameter $\gamma$ in the form $e^{-\gamma(H_{prob}-E_{min})}$ creates strong non-convexity as $\gamma$ grows. To address this, we introduce a new strategy that replaces the original objective with a Bayesian framework to generate a well-mixed posterior distribution over $E_{min}$ for inclusion in the optimization. By utilizing distributional estimation techniques such as the Expectation Maximization (EM) or Cross-Entropy Method (CeM), we achieve a well-mixed exploration of the parameter space, thereby improving the probability of escaping local minima. Experiments across random graphs and instances of the traveling salesman problem show that this method outperforms both standard and other techniques across the Convergence, True Objective (TC), and Approximate Ratio in instances of parameter $\gamma$. Finally, our approach achieves a significantly higher overlap between the ground and excited states compared with conventional techniques.

This paper presents an algorithm for identifying the connected components of the simultaneous subspaces defined by a set of ellipse parameters, with each region represented as a union of ellipse intersections. The initial step involves locating all pairwise intersection points between the ellipses; since the count of these points is at most O(n²), the arrangement formed by their boundaries possesses O(n²) vertices. Consequently, the arrangement is realized through a standard planar graph representation before its connected components are computed. The resulting regions are subsequently stored in a compact format, achieving both a geometric description and an efficient data structure representation.

We investigate an extension of the triangular-lattice Hubbard model that incorporates next-nearest-neighbor (J_{NN}) hopping within the spin-channel. Initially, mean-field analysis indicates that increasing this term enhances the magnetic bond associated with staggered flux patterns. Subsequently, we conduct a comprehensive study of the phasal landscape of a half-filled system, utilizing density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) techniques on narrow cylinders complemented by quantum Monte-Carlo (QMC) simulations on a square lattice. These calculations, performed in the limit where vertical next-vertical hopping is maximized, reveal a complex interplay between stripe and uniform magnetic phases that closely mirrors observations regarding stagger magnetism. A key finding is the emergence of an ordered phase in a wide parameter range, characterized by long-range order of the stagger flux state. Furthermore, our results offer compelling evidence for the "order-by-disorder" phenomenon, where thermal fluctuations select a specific low symmetry state.

Accurately diagnosing degenerative conditions like degenerative disc disease and spondylolisthesis is crucial for clinical decision support; however, this task is labor-intensive and subject to interobserver variability when performed manually. This study presents an efficient framework for quantizing these conditions using computed tomography (CT). The core algorithm localizes each vertebra independently and performs labeling through a two-stage process: initially, it rectifies the spine within a slice, aligning it horizontally, and subsequently applies an anatomically constrained statistical model to facilitate labeling, which is normally challenging in misaligned images. Since vertebral localization and recognition rely on adjacent anatomical cues, the approach incorporates a weighted combination of these features. Specifically, weighting is determined by calculating the geometric distance between an image and an ideal statistical model of vertebral alignment and labeling, giving rectified images a significantly lower distance metric compared to unrectified ones. This technique leverages pre-operatively acquired CTs to automatically generate reliable measurements of spinal degeneration. The study includes experimental validation on a SAG-optimized image set, and preliminary results using 70 non-operatively acquired images from Lumbosacral CT scans are presented.

We investigate an integrable stochastic gradient descent (SDPGN) model for learning a function from data, where the input consists of graphs with random weights and the output node values are sampled from a Gaussian distribution independent of the structure. We prove that, in a large system limit, the empirical risk converges to a deterministic function of a measure known as asymptotic data. This data is constructed from two infinite measures defined on a combinatorial set derived from the graph's local structures. Because these measures depend only on the graph and the input/output distributions separately, they constitute the asymptotic data.

Assuming the graph entries are independent and identically distributed random variables with a subgaussian distribution, our analysis shows that this model's asymptotic data is independent of the specific independence assumption and the subgaussian tail of the matrix entries in the limit of large systems, reducing to a much simpler form. We also demonstrate that this asymptotic data accurately captures the limit behavior of other statistical quantities related to learning, such as generalization error and training loss. In this case, we find that the limit of the stochastic gradient descent process can be described by a deterministic dynamical system in the large system limit, where the dynamics are driven by the asymptotic data.

We introduce the concept of a relative quantum topology for a Kähler manifold relative to a given algebraic alteration. This framework allows the reconstruction of the relative (partial) quantum cohomring and the associated Witten-Verlinde algebra. Central components include the derivation of a relative (partial) Atiyah-Classes, a (partial) relative Chern class, and a (partial) relative Donaldson-Thomas polynomial. These tools enable the examination of how a relative (partial) quantum product and the associated algebra evolve across the alteration, with an additional exploration into K-theory and the relative $K$-theory of a map serving as the (partial) basis.

When two piezoelectric materials are positioned near one another without a common support, acoustic waves generated in the first can transmit entirely to the second. Although these materials do not share a physical bond, full transmission occurs because the air surrounding both supports mechanical interactions capable of conveying acoustic energy. Consequently, the air acts as an intermediate structural element within this configuration. Experimental findings confirm that nearly 100% of acoustic power reaches the second crystal under specific conditions defined by the separation distance between the crystals and the frequency of the wave. When the separation equals one-quarter of the wave's wavelength (a standing wave loop), transmission reaches complete levels, whereas other distances result in power retention at source levels. Furthermore, by rotating one crystal relative to the other, the intensity of transmission can be controlled.

It is widely established that optical nonlinearity in liquids can function as a non-invasive method to access system information, often compared to a non-linear optical reservoir. In this study, we explore the possibility of utilizing nonlinear optics with exciton-polaritons to probe out-of-equilibrium quantum information within liquid environments. We demonstrate that even at the absolute minimum concentration, where quantum effects dominate, there is strong coupling between the optical cavity and the emitter, and the system's behavior can be accurately described using nonlinear quantum state process Vectors (VSS). Furthermore, we explore how to employ Gaussian states and optimize measurement strategies to achieve accurate reconstructions through photon counting techniques. Ultimately, our work introduces a new approach for applying quantum technologies through reservoir optics.

We introduce a broad class of splices and blow-ups that preserve the coherent structure of formalized singular spaces, alongside another category of splices and blow-ups for which the coherent property may fail. To analyze coherent singularity, we establish a fundamental link between a singularity's coherence and the flatness (specifically, relative smoothness) of its critical stratum within a relative resolution.

This paper explores how Galileo's background as a skilled mathematician influenced his philosophical contributions to science. It addresses his views on deductive versus inductive reasoning and the relationship between the human mind and the universe within his major works, specifically the *Dialogue* and *Discourse on Method*. The analysis highlights a consistent alignment between Galileo's mathematical and philosophical frameworks, countering the view that his reliance on sensory experience and a belief in a law-bound cosmos represented a radical break from traditional scholasticism. Instead, his scholastic inheritance persisted, modified only by his unique integration of the intellectual limits imposed by a focus on empirical evidence with the scholastic system. Consequently, scholasticism evolved into an empirically grounded approach to studying nature. Ultimately, Galileo's science was defined by his synthesis of inherited traditions and his emphasis on observation and experimentation.

Recombination is a pivotal event in the early universe, leading to the rapid collapse of ionized hydrogen to a neutral state within a non-equilibrium framework, a period conventionally described using Gaussian models. In this work, we investigate the effects of the non-Gaussian component introduced by Saha ionization on the primordial structure's power spectrum. To achieve this, we employ an analytical method to compute the skewness term and subsequently apply the Padé approximation technique to evaluate its contribution. Our findings suggest that ignoring the non-Gaussian component may result in a ~1% discrepancy on the power spectrum at k = 0.004. Additionally, while previous research indicates that the power spectrum during recombination is nearly scale-invariant, our specific results demonstrate a slight increase in amplitude on small scales.

A hybrid simulation using embedded model 1D magnetic islands demonstrates that adding particles into an MHD framework accurately predicts the sizes of merging islands introduced by perturbations. Specifically, a q=2.5 rational surface was displaced using a localized current profile spike applied via magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) with adaptively integrated particle-in-Cell code. While initial displacement of the q=2.5 surface correlates with particle injection, final merging is governed by MHD evolution of a perturbed current flux. This research reveals that while particle effects significantly influence the growth phase of magnetic islands, the ultimate coalescence reverts to classical magnetohydrodynamic behavior.
